RagShortTexts: Barcelona's maritime trade depends on contracts, freight and shipboard responsibilities.
Storms, piracy and embargoes expose merchants and crews to different losses.

Variants.Content: Barcelona was the commercial engine of the Crown of Aragon, and its harbour was built around trade as much as war. The Drassanes shipyards were among the major medieval naval arsenals of the western Mediterranean, and they turned out war galleys and merchant vessels. Catalan merchants ran galley routes to Sicily, North Africa, and the Levant, carrying wool, cloth, and grain outward and bringing spices and dyes home. The Consolat de Mar tribunal settled disputes between merchants according to written maritime custom, and its principles spread to other Mediterranean ports. Port dues paid for the walls, the shipwrights, and the royal treasury, so the crown had every reason to protect the routes that filled its coffers.

Catalan merchants exported fine woolens, saffron, and weapons, establishing profitable trading outposts in Sicily and Alexandria. Sailors loaded their galleys at the city quays under written contracts that set out freight and crew duties. Storms, pirates, and sudden royal embargoes could ruin a cargo before it reached market.
